findings.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (record.save) inside a model validation, breaking the pure-validation contract; validations run multiple times per signup causing match_count double-counting, and a failed record.save return value is silently swallowed

Unconditional DB query on every email validation via BlockedEmail.should_block? adds a per-request remote lookup to a previously cache-guarded in-memory path, affecting all user-validating flows even on sites with no blocked_emails rows

Email validator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and only covers the blocked-email branch, leaving whitelist, blacklist, and error-suppression interaction logic untested, so a regex regression would go undetected by CI
BlockedEmail table/model ships with no writer (no admin UI, rake task, seed, or API), making the blocking feature inert in production since the table can only be populated via raw SQL
Validator placement in lib/validators/ may cause NameError at boot if lib is not in Rails autoload/eager-load paths, since validates resolves EmailValidator at User class load time
The blocked_emails table has no writer anywhere in the diff (no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed), so operators cannot actually block an email address and the feature is inert in production

The new spec covers only the BlockedEmail.should_block? branch and stubs it out; the transplanted whitelist/blacklist restriction logic (email_in_restriction_setting?, dot-escaping, Regexp construction) has zero assertions, so regressions in it would pass the suite
The new errors: and values: JSON fields in users_controller have no request/controller spec, leaving the client's dependency on result.errors.email and result.values.email unverified end-to-end
When a rejected email is retyped, the client shows the generic 'user.email.invalid' message instead of the server's specific blocked message, giving the user a wrong reason on retry
should_block? performs writes (record.save) inside a validation hook, inflating match_count stats on repeated validations and risking 500s or corrupt/locked stats under concurrent rejected signups

The email_changed? guard on validates :email means the new BlockedEmail check is skipped when email is unchanged, so emails added to the blocklist after account creation are never checked on subsequent saves

values: user.attributes.slice(...) returns persisted attribute values rather than the submitted form values, so a normalized email could fail to match the typed accountEmail in rejectedEmails, silently disabling retry validation
BlockedEmail mechanism has no writer anywhere in the diff (no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, seed, or migration), so should_block? always returns false in production and the feature is dead code
match_count/last_match_at statistics tracking performs record.save inside model validation, causing write side effects on every validation call including failed/rolled-back saves
The do_nothing action type and action_type Enum are speculative generality with no requirement behind them, adding unnecessary branches and schema surface
Frontend create_account_controller discards the server's specific error reason and substitutes generic 'user.email.invalid' message, so blocked-email users get no actionable error
users_controller response payload change (errors, values) is a general API surface expansion affecting all failed account creations, with the values hash having no consumer (dead payload)

Client-side rejectedEmails exact-string matching never expires and ignores case, causing stale client-side rejections that diverge from server state (e.g., rejections persist after admin unblocks an email)
BlockedEmail.should_block? performs non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count causing lost-update races under concurrent signups
match_count increment happens inside model validation, so when the surrounding User save fails/rolls back, match_count and last_match_at statistics are silently discarded
BlockedEmail lookup is case-sensitive while email identity is case-insensitive per RFC, allowing blocklist bypass via capitalization and duplicate rows despite unique index
blocked_emails table has no writer (no admin UI, rake task, seed, or API endpoint), leaving the feature dead in production
User email presence and uniqueness validations are now conditional on email_changed?, so unchanged emails skip validation and pre-existing duplicates or NULLs persist silently
Error-type coupling in EmailValidator short-circuits should_block? when a domain error exists, suppressing the blocked check and its statistics
Client/server canonical-form drift on rejectedEmails: server returns persisted attribute while client compares raw input, so normalization divergence breaks the instant-reject
No spec exercises the real integration path; all tests stub boundaries, leaving the validator wiring unverified
EmailValidator in lib/ relies on lib being in the autoload path, risking NameError at first use; should be moved to app/validators or autoload verified
Missing terminal newline in lib/validators/email_validator.rb

Client-side rejected-email cache treats all email errors as 'invalid', mislabeling pre-existing error types (uniqueness, whitelist/blacklist) and silently changing the user-facing error contract; condition should discriminate on the specific blocked error key

BlockedEmail.should_block? check is skipped whenever a restriction error exists due to validation ordering, so match_count/last_match_at statistics are not recorded for emails also caught by the domain blacklist

The email_changed? conditional gate carried over from the old email_validator causes blocked_emails to not be consulted on profile saves when email is unchanged, so blocked emails added after signup pass validation
BlockedEmail lookup compares raw un-normalized email without downcasing/trimming, so case variation bypasses the blocklist
Case-sensitive unique index on blocked_emails.email allows same address stored twice in different cases
New BlockedEmail path is strictly weaker than the case-insensitive email_in_restriction_setting? regex
should_block? performs DB read and write (record.save) inside ActiveModel validation, turning validation into an unthrottled write path for anonymous attackers
Counter update on blocked_emails races concurrent saves with no lock, causing lost updates and inflated match_count
last_match_at/counter updated even when surrounding user save fails, making stats meaningless
SiteSetting domain string interpolated directly into Regexp.new with only dots escaped, allowing ReDoS and silent meaning changes from regex metacharacters
Failure response echoes user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email") back to unauthenticated client, a mild information disclosure/reflection surface

BlockedEmail validator path in email_validator_spec.rb is tested only against a stub of should_block?, never exercising real DB lookup, block gate, or save side effect; a regression passing wrong value to should_block? passes tests

No test covers the short-circuit interaction in email_validator.rb:18 where existing whitelist/blacklist restriction errors suppress the blocked check and should_block? write; the restriction-setting half of the validator is untested and an inverted blank? guard passes all tests
should_block? uses exact case-sensitive match while legacy restriction regex is case-insensitive, and no test exercises case variance, so mixed-case blocked emails silently no-op

last_match_at null test is a mirror test asserting DB column defaults/migration nullability rather than observable blocking semantics, costing a DB round-trip for an assertion that can only fail on a migration defect
Migration creates blocked_emails table but no writer (seed, rake task, admin UI, or API) exists in the diff, so feature ships inert with zero blocking behavior
should_block? performs write-on-every-signup-attempt side effects (match_count/last_match_at updates) that can never fire since nothing writes to the table

Email restriction check moved to a global EachValidator that runs for every model declaring validates :email, email: true, introducing hidden coupling where any adopting model gets BlockedEmail side-effect writes on the validation read path
should_block? performs a save inside validation, so validation performs uncommitted DB writes and can persist/update a record as a side effect of validating an object that never saves
Two simultaneous signup attempts for the same blocked email both read and write back match_count, causing a lost update with no concurrency guard, making match statistics unreliable

Lookup case-sensitivity differs between old and new blocking mechanisms: legacy blacklist matched case-insensitively but BlockedEmail.where(email: email) in PostgreSQL is case-sensitive, so blocked rows can be bypassed via case variation
No migration exists to normalize email case on load into blocked_emails, making the case-sensitivity drift undetectable until someone evades a block
BlockedEmail.should_block? performs DB read-then-write inside model validator with bare record.save whose failure is silently swallowed, undercounting block-rate telemetry
should_block? mutates and persists BlockedEmail rows during validation of an unrelated record, inflating match_count/last_match_at on validation paths that never commit
Blocked email lookup is an exact case-sensitive string match with no email normalization, allowing blocked users to register with case-variant addresses
Client-side rejectedEmails.contains(email) is an exact string match with no trim/normalization, so the inline rejection hint only fires for byte-identical retries

New errors/values payload shape depends on result.values being present; on failure paths like ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid the JS silently skips the rejection-memory push, making the feature partial
Regexp.new builds a regex from raw admin-entered email_domains_blacklist text with no RegexpError guard, turning malformed config into site-wide 500s on all signups
New spec file tests neither the regex construction nor the blacklist/whitelist branches, leaving a coverage gap on the only non-trivial logic added

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

per_golden_matches.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both describe that the `should_block`/`should_block_email?` check is not a pure read: it mutates/persists `BlockedEmail` records by updating match statistics (`match_count`/`last_match_at`) during a blocking check, which is a misleading side effect and can be problematic under concurrency/validation paths.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both describe the same core issue: the blocklist email lookup is case-sensitive, so a differently-capitalized email (e.g., User@Example.com) can bypass a block entry for user@example.com, enabling blocked-user access. Candidate adds extra detail about duplicates/unique index but aligns with the golden concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (record.save) inside a model validation, breaking the pure-validation contract; validations run multiple times per signup causing match_count double-counting, and a failed record.save return value is silently swallowed

Unconditional DB query on every email validation via BlockedEmail.should_block? adds a per-request remote lookup to a previously cache-guarded in-memory path, affecting all user-validating flows even on sites with no blocked_emails rows

adjudication.rationale: The new `EmailValidator#validate_each` unconditionally calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` whenever no prior email error exists (`record.errors[attribute].blank?`). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, i.e., a DB query, even when the `blocked_emails` table is empty. Previously, email validation logic in `User#email_validator` only checked site settings with a regex and did not hit the DB. This is a diff-grounded performance/architecture regression rather than a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Email validator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and only covers the blocked-email branch, leaving whitelist, blacklist, and error-suppression interaction logic untested, so a regex regression would go undetected by CI

adjudication.rationale: The new `EmailValidator` contains nontrivial logic beyond the blocked-email check: whitelist/blacklist domain matching via `email_in_restriction_setting?` (regex built from `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist`), and the suppression rule `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` which prevents blocked-email checks when a prior whitelist/blacklist error exists. However, `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and asserts presence/absence of errors for that branch, without any coverage for whitelist/blacklist regex behavior or the interaction/suppression condition. This is a specific, diff-grounded test gap (not a direct runtime bug).

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail table/model ships with no writer (no admin UI, rake task, seed, or API), making the blocking feature inert in production since the table can only be populated via raw SQL

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a BlockedEmail model/table and enforces blocking via the new EmailValidator (BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)), but it does not add any codepath to create/manage BlockedEmail records (no controller/API/admin UI/seed/rake task shown). As a result, in a default deployment the table would remain empty unless populated out-of-band, making the new blocking capability effectively unused unless admins write directly to the DB.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Validator placement in lib/validators/ may cause NameError at boot if lib is not in Rails autoload/eager-load paths, since validates resolves EmailValidator at User class load time

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a custom ActiveModel validator at `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` and immediately uses it in `app/models/user.rb` via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`. That requires the `EmailValidator` constant to be loadable when `User` is loaded. Whether `lib/validators` is in Rails autoload/eager-load paths isn’t shown in the diff, so a boot-time `NameError` isn’t verifiable here, but it’s a concrete, diff-grounded integration concern to confirm (autoload/eager_load or explicit require).

adjudication_records.issue_text: The blocked_emails table has no writer anywhere in the diff (no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed), so operators cannot actually block an email address and the feature is inert in production

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, `blocked_emails` is introduced (migration + `BlockedEmail` model) and enforced via the new `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but there is no diff-visible mechanism to populate/manage `blocked_emails` in normal operation (no controller/admin UI/API/rake/seed changes shown). That makes the feature operationally incomplete unless records are inserted out-of-band (console/DB). This is a real, diff-grounded scope/operability concern, not a correctness bug in the blocking logic itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The new spec covers only the BlockedEmail.should_block? branch and stubs it out; the transplanted whitelist/blacklist restriction logic (email_in_restriction_setting?, dot-escaping, Regexp construction) has zero assertions, so regressions in it would pass the suite

adjudication.rationale: In `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`, the only assertions exercise the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` path, and that call is stubbed (`BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?)...`). The new/transplanted whitelist/blacklist restriction logic in `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` (`email_in_restriction_setting?`, `setting.gsub('.', '\.')`, `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)`) is not covered by any spec shown in the diff, so regressions there would not be caught.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The new errors: and values: JSON fields in users_controller have no request/controller spec, leaving the client's dependency on result.errors.email and result.values.email unverified end-to-end

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new JSON fields in `UsersController#create` error response (`errors: user.errors.to_hash`, `values: user.attributes.slice(...)`) and the Ember client now relies on them (`if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... result.values.email ... }`). The added specs cover `BlockedEmail` and `EmailValidator`, but there is no request/controller spec in the diff asserting the `create` endpoint returns `errors`/`values` in the failure case, so the client-server contract isn’t verified end-to-end.

adjudication_records.issue_text: When a rejected email is retyped, the client shows the generic 'user.email.invalid' message instead of the server's specific blocked message, giving the user a wrong reason on retry

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, `emailValidation` now short-circuits when `rejectedEmails` contains the typed email and returns `failed: true` with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`. On create failure, the controller pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` whenever `result.errors.email` exists, but it does not preserve the server-provided error message (e.g. `user.email.blocked` from the new `EmailValidator`). This makes a retried blocked email show the generic 'invalid' message instead of the specific blocked reason.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? performs writes (record.save) inside a validation hook, inflating match_count stats on repeated validations and risking 500s or corrupt/locked stats under concurrent rejected signups

The email_changed? guard on validates :email means the new BlockedEmail check is skipped when email is unchanged, so emails added to the blocklist after account creation are never checked on subsequent saves

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/user.rb` the new validator `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` means the `EmailValidator` (which calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`) only runs when `email_changed?` is true. So if a user is saved without changing their email, the new blocklist check will not be re-evaluated. This is a real, diff-grounded behavioral limitation, but it’s not clearly a defect since the same `email_changed?` guard existed before (the new block logic is primarily for signup/changes).

adjudication_records.issue_text: values: user.attributes.slice(...) returns persisted attribute values rather than the submitted form values, so a normalized email could fail to match the typed accountEmail in rejectedEmails, silently disabling retry validation

adjudication.rationale: In `UsersController#create`, the `values` field is built from `user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` on the *unsaved* `user` object in the failure path. From the diff, there’s no indication these are “persisted” values; they are the in-memory attributes that were assigned from the submitted params (plus any in-memory mutations). The claim that this necessarily returns persisted values and causes a normalized-email mismatch with `accountEmail`/`rejectedEmails` is not verifiable from the diff (no shown normalization/downcasing logic).

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail mechanism has no writer anywhere in the diff (no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, seed, or migration), so should_block? always returns false in production and the feature is dead code

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail` (model + migration) and uses it via `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in the new `EmailValidator`, but the diff does not include any code path to create/populate `blocked_emails` records (no controller/admin UI/seed/rake task). So the feature is effectively unusable unless records are inserted out-of-band (e.g., rails console/manual DB), meaning the reviewer concern about “no writer in this diff” is valid; however it’s not strictly a runtime defect because the table can still be populated manually.

adjudication_records.issue_text: match_count/last_match_at statistics tracking performs record.save inside model validation, causing write side effects on every validation call including failed/rolled-back saves

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a write side effect during validation: `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, and `BlockedEmail.should_block?` unconditionally increments `match_count`/sets `last_match_at` and calls `record.save` whenever a matching `BlockedEmail` exists. This means validating a User email (even when the User ultimately fails validation or the save is rolled back) will still persist changes to the `blocked_emails` table, and repeated validation calls will keep writing. That’s a concrete, diff-grounded design/architecture concern rather than a clearly unintended defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The do_nothing action type and action_type Enum are speculative generality with no requirement behind them, adding unnecessary branches and schema surface

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce an `action_type` column plus an `Enum` with `:block` and `:do_nothing` (see `BlockedEmail.actions` and `should_block?`), but the finding’s core claim—“no requirement behind them” / “unnecessary”—can’t be verified from the diff alone. The code and specs explicitly support both action types, so it’s not a concrete, diff-verifiable issue like a bug or an incomplete implementation; it’s a subjective product/requirements judgment not provable here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Frontend create_account_controller discards the server's specific error reason and substitutes generic 'user.email.invalid' message, so blocked-email users get no actionable error

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show the client-side inline validation can replace a server-provided email error with a generic one: on failed create, `rejectedEmails.pushObject(result.values.email)` stores only the email (not the specific error), and later `emailValidation` returns `failed: true` with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` whenever the email is in `rejectedEmails`. However, the server’s specific reason is not entirely discarded because the controller still flashes `result.message` (now built from `user.errors.full_messages`, which would include the new `user.email.blocked` message). So the issue is primarily about losing specificity in inline field validation/UX rather than a functional defect where users get no error at all.

adjudication_records.issue_text: users_controller response payload change (errors, values) is a general API surface expansion affecting all failed account creations, with the values hash having no consumer (dead payload)

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a direct consumer of the new `values` payload: in `create_account_controller.js`, on failed account creation it checks `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values)` and then uses `result.values.email` to push into `rejectedEmails`. Therefore `values` is not dead/unused. While the controller response does expand the failure JSON (`errors`, `values`), the specific claim that `values` has no consumer is contradicted by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client-side rejectedEmails exact-string matching never expires and ignores case, causing stale client-side rejections that diverge from server state (e.g., rejections persist after admin unblocks an email)

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a `rejectedEmails` array on the client (`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])`) and short-circuits email validation if it `contains(email)` by immediately returning `failed: true` with `user.email.invalid`. Entries are added on any server-side create failure that includes `result.errors.email` (`pushObject(result.values.email)`), and there is no code to clear/expire this list or re-check server state. This can cause the client to keep rejecting an email within the same session even if the server would later accept it (e.g., after an admin unblocks it), creating a client/server divergence. The “ignores case” part is not clearly verifiable from the diff (server-side matching/canonicalization isn’t shown), but the never-expiring stale rejection behavior is directly implied by the added code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count causing lost-update races under concurrent signups

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb, BlockedEmail.should_block? does `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` then `record.match_count += 1` and `record.save`. Under concurrent calls for the same email, two processes can read the same match_count and both write back the same incremented value, losing one update. This non-atomic read-modify-write can make match_count/last_match_at inaccurate (data integrity issue) during concurrent signups.

adjudication_records.issue_text: match_count increment happens inside model validation, so when the surrounding User save fails/rolls back, match_count and last_match_at statistics are silently discarded

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, the statistics update happens in `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which explicitly does `record.save` on the `BlockedEmail` record (app/models/blocked_email.rb). That save is a separate persistence operation from the surrounding `User` validation/save, and nothing in the shown diff indicates it’s wrapped in a broader transaction that would roll it back. So the claim that `match_count`/`last_match_at` are “silently discarded” when the `User` save fails is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail lookup is case-sensitive while email identity is case-insensitive per RFC, allowing blocklist bypass via capitalization and duplicate rows despite unique index
matched_golden_ids: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same core issue: the blocklist email lookup is case-sensitive, so a differently-capitalized email (e.g., User@Example.com) can bypass a block entry for user@example.com, enabling blocked-user access. Candidate adds extra detail about duplicates/unique index but aligns with the golden concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: blocked_emails table has no writer (no admin UI, rake task, seed, or API endpoint), leaving the feature dead in production

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `blocked_emails` table/model and enforces it in `EmailValidator` via `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, but within this diff there is no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed code added to populate/manage `blocked_emails`. Without some external mechanism (not shown here), the feature would be effectively inert because no records would exist to match.

adjudication_records.issue_text: User email presence and uniqueness validations are now conditional on email_changed?, so unchanged emails skip validation and pre-existing duplicates or NULLs persist silently

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/user.rb the new presence and uniqueness validations for email are unconditional (`validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true`). Only the custom email-domain/blocked-email validator is conditional (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). The finding incorrectly claims presence/uniqueness were made conditional on `email_changed?`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Error-type coupling in EmailValidator short-circuits should_block? when a domain error exists, suppressing the blocked check and its statistics

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email check is gated by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. This means if the whitelist/blacklist logic above adds an `:email` error, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is never called, so its side effects (incrementing `match_count` and setting `last_match_at` in `BlockedEmail.should_block?`) won’t run for those emails. That’s a real, diff-grounded coupling/observability concern, but it’s not clearly a correctness defect without a requirement that blocked-email stats must be tracked even when other validation errors exist.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client/server canonical-form drift on rejectedEmails: server returns persisted attribute while client compares raw input, so normalization divergence breaks the instant-reject

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the client caches `result.values.email` (from `user.attributes.slice(...)`) into `rejectedEmails` and later compares it to the current `accountEmail` string. However, nothing in the shown server-side changes normalizes/canonicalizes email (no downcasing/stripping/etc.), and `user.attributes` on a failed create is not a “persisted attribute” but simply the assigned value. The new `EmailValidator` also operates on the passed-in `value` directly. Any canonical-form drift would depend on unseen code outside this diff, so the specific claim isn’t verifiable from the provided changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No spec exercises the real integration path; all tests stub boundaries, leaving the validator wiring unverified

adjudication.rationale: The new validator wiring is introduced in `User` via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, but the added specs only test `EmailValidator#validate_each` in isolation and stub the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` boundary (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`). While `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb` exercises `BlockedEmail.should_block?` against the DB, there is no spec that validates a `User` and asserts the `EmailValidator` actually runs (i.e., end-to-end wiring/integration of model + validator + blocked email behavior).

adjudication_records.issue_text: EmailValidator in lib/ relies on lib being in the autoload path, risking NameError at first use; should be moved to app/validators or autoload verified

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` and then relies on it via `validates :email, email: true` in `app/models/user.rb`. Rails will only resolve `EmailValidator` if `lib` (and `lib/validators`) is on the autoload/eager-load path, but this diff does not show any configuration ensuring that. This is a concrete, diff-grounded concern about class loading/placement, though the diff alone can’t confirm whether Discourse already autoloads `lib`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Missing terminal newline in lib/validators/email_validator.rb

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly shows “\ No newline at end of file” for lib/validators/email_validator.rb, so the observation is true, but it’s a formatting/style nit rather than a functional defect or substantive review issue per the category definitions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client-side rejected-email cache treats all email errors as 'invalid', mislabeling pre-existing error types (uniqueness, whitelist/blacklist) and silently changing the user-facing error contract; condition should discriminate on the specific blocked error key

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any failed signup response that includes `result.errors.email` causes the submitted email to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (`pushObject(result.values.email)`), regardless of the specific error type (blocked/not_allowed/uniqueness/etc.). On subsequent validations, `emailValidation` checks `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and immediately returns `failed: true` with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, which overrides/mislabels the original server-side error and changes the user-facing error behavior for that email. This is directly introduced by the diff and is incorrect behavior for non-"invalid" email errors.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? check is skipped whenever a restriction error exists due to validation ordering, so match_count/last_match_at statistics are not recorded for emails also caught by the domain blacklist

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is only called when `record.errors[attribute].blank?` (i.e., after whitelist/blacklist checks add no error). Therefore, if an email is rejected by the domain whitelist/blacklist, `should_block?` is never invoked and its side effects (`match_count`/`last_match_at` updates in `BlockedEmail.should_block?`) will not occur for those emails. This is a real, diff-grounded behavioral gap affecting statistics collection, but it’s not necessarily a functional defect unless the intent was to always record stats regardless of other validation failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The email_changed? conditional gate carried over from the old email_validator causes blocked_emails to not be consulted on profile saves when email is unchanged, so blocked emails added after signup pass validation

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/user.rb` the new validator is still gated by `if: :email_changed?` (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). Since `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is only consulted inside `EmailValidator#validate_each` (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`), that blocked-email check will not run on saves where the user’s email is unchanged. This means an email that becomes blocked after signup won’t be revalidated on unrelated profile updates—an edge-case/scope concern rather than a clearly verifiable defect from the diff alone (it may be intentional to avoid invalidating existing users).

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail lookup compares raw un-normalized email without downcasing/trimming, so case variation bypasses the blocklist

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` does an exact-match query `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with whatever `value` is passed from `EmailValidator#validate_each` (and later from the client via `result.values.email`). The diff shows no normalization (e.g., `strip`/`downcase`) when storing blocked emails or when validating user input, so a blocked entry like `bad@spam.com` would not match `Bad@Spam.com` or ` bad@spam.com `, allowing blocklist bypass via case/whitespace variation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Case-sensitive unique index on blocked_emails.email allows same address stored twice in different cases

adjudication.rationale: The migration adds a plain unique index on `blocked_emails.email` (`add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true`) and the model uses `validates :email, ... uniqueness: true` with no `case_sensitive: false`. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` also does an exact match lookup (`where(email: email)`), so two rows differing only by case can exist (and lookups can miss), allowing the same address to be stored/treated differently by case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New BlockedEmail path is strictly weaker than the case-insensitive email_in_restriction_setting? regex

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting?`, the restriction match uses a case-insensitive regexp (`Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)`), but the new blocked-email check calls `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is an exact equality match and will typically be case-sensitive (e.g., on Postgres) unless emails are normalized elsewhere (not shown in the diff). This makes blocked-email enforcement weaker/easier to bypass via casing differences compared to the existing restriction logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? performs DB read and write (record.save) inside ActiveModel validation, turning validation into an unthrottled write path for anonymous attackers

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the model validation calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when validating `:email`. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (new in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`) performs a DB read (`where(...).first`) and, on match, mutates and persists the record (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`). Since this runs during `User` validation (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` in `app/models/user.rb`), an unauthenticated signup attempt using a known blocked email will trigger a write on every validation, creating an unthrottled write path that can be abused for DB write amplification/DoS.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Counter update on blocked_emails races concurrent saves with no lock, causing lost updates and inflated match_count

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code does a read-modify-write increment (`record.match_count += 1; record.save`) with no locking or atomic SQL update. Concurrent calls can overwrite each other, causing lost increments and incorrect `match_count`/`last_match_at` statistics. (The finding’s “inflated” wording is off—this pattern typically undercounts—but the race/correctness issue is real and diff-grounded.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: last_match_at/counter updated even when surrounding user save fails, making stats meaningless

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#validate_each`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is called during validation and, if a matching record exists, it increments `match_count` and sets `last_match_at`, then `record.save` persists those changes (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `app/models/blocked_email.rb`). This side-effect happens regardless of whether the surrounding `User` ultimately saves successfully (it may fail later due to other validation errors), so the blocked-email stats can be incremented for failed user creations. That’s a real, diff-grounded concern, but whether it’s “meaningless” depends on intended semantics (counting attempts vs. successful creations), so it’s not a clearly verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: SiteSetting domain string interpolated directly into Regexp.new with only dots escaped, allowing ReDoS and silent meaning changes from regex metacharacters

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `email_in_restriction_setting?` builds `regexp = Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` where `domains` comes from `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist` with only `.` escaped via `setting.gsub('.', '\.')`. Other regex metacharacters in the setting (e.g., `(`, `|`, `*`, `+`, `{}`) are not escaped, so the setting can silently change the regex meaning and can enable pathological regexes (ReDoS risk) when validating emails.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Failure response echoes user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email") back to unauthenticated client, a mild information disclosure/reflection surface

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` to the JSON failure response in `UsersController#create`, but those fields come from the just-built `user` record (i.e., the same values the unauthenticated client submitted). Nothing in the diff shows any additional sensitive server-side data being exposed (no IDs, tokens, or other users’ attributes), and the frontend uses `result.values.email` only to cache rejected inputs. So the claim of “information disclosure” beyond reflecting the requester’s own input isn’t supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail validator path in email_validator_spec.rb is tested only against a stub of should_block?, never exercising real DB lookup, block gate, or save side effect; a regression passing wrong value to should_block? passes tests

adjudication.rationale: In `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`, the “blocked email” behavior is exercised only by stubbing `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (`BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?).with(record.email)...`), so it does not cover the real DB lookup/stat updates in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (incrementing `match_count`, setting `last_match_at`, `save`). That said, the claim that “passing wrong value to should_block? passes tests” is not accurate here because the stub is constrained with `.with(record.email)`, which would fail if `EmailValidator` called `should_block?` with a different argument. There is also a separate `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb` that covers the real side effects, but there’s no integration test of validator + real `BlockedEmail.should_block?`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test covers the short-circuit interaction in email_validator.rb:18 where existing whitelist/blacklist restriction errors suppress the blocked check and should_block? write; the restriction-setting half of the validator is untested and an inverted blank? guard passes all tests

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb the blocked-email check is guarded by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, so any whitelist/blacklist error added earlier will suppress calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (and thus suppress its match_count/last_match_at side effects). The added spec (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) only stubs/asserts the blocked-email path and does not test whitelist/blacklist behavior or this short-circuit interaction, so the restriction-setting half is effectively untested and a guard inversion could slip by.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? uses exact case-sensitive match while legacy restriction regex is case-insensitive, and no test exercises case variance, so mixed-case blocked emails silently no-op

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block? does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is an exact match (case-sensitive on common DBs like PostgreSQL) and BlockedEmail validates uniqueness without case-insensitive handling. In contrast, the legacy domain restriction check builds a case-insensitive regex (`Regexp.new(..., true)`). There is no normalization/downcasing shown in this diff, and the added specs only cover exact-case matches, so mixed-case emails in either the blocked list or user input can fail to block unexpectedly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: last_match_at null test is a mirror test asserting DB column defaults/migration nullability rather than observable blocking semantics, costing a DB round-trip for an assertion that can only fail on a migration defect

adjudication.rationale: The spec explicitly frames `last_match_at` being `nil` on a newly created `BlockedEmail` as intended observable model semantics (“have ever been blocked by looking at last_match_at”), not just a migration-nullability mirror. In the diff, no model callback sets `last_match_at`, so the test is a straightforward behavior check that could also catch future code changes (not only migration defects). The “costing a DB round-trip for an assertion that can only fail on a migration defect” claim is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Migration creates blocked_emails table but no writer (seed, rake task, admin UI, or API) exists in the diff, so feature ships inert with zero blocking behavior

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `blocked_emails` persistence (migration/model) and enforcement (`EmailValidator` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?`), but it does not add any way in this diff to populate/manage `blocked_emails` (no seed, rake task, controller/admin UI/API). As a result, the blocking behavior will only take effect if records are inserted out-of-band (e.g., console/manual SQL), making the feature effectively inactive by default rather than a runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? performs write-on-every-signup-attempt side effects (match_count/last_match_at updates) that can never fire since nothing writes to the table

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly wires `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` into email validation via the new `EmailValidator` (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). `should_block?` will execute on signup attempts and its side effects (incrementing `match_count`/setting `last_match_at`) *do* fire whenever a matching `blocked_emails` row exists. While this diff doesn’t add a UI/seed path to populate `blocked_emails`, it does add the model + migration, and the claim that the side effects “can never fire since nothing writes to the table” is not verifiable from the diff and is too absolute given the table can be populated externally (e.g., console/admin tooling not shown).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Email restriction check moved to a global EachValidator that runs for every model declaring validates :email, email: true, introducing hidden coupling where any adopting model gets BlockedEmail side-effect writes on the validation read path

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a global `EmailValidator < ActiveModel::EachValidator` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) that, after domain allow/deny checks, calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. `should_block?` performs side-effect writes (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) on the validation path (app/models/blocked_email.rb). Any model that opts into `validates :email, email: true` will implicitly incur these DB writes, creating hidden coupling beyond the original `User#email_validator` method that was removed and replaced with `validates :email, email: true` (app/models/user.rb). This is a real architecture/scope concern grounded in the diff, not a direct functional defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? performs a save inside validation, so validation performs uncommitted DB writes and can persist/update a record as a side effect of validating an object that never saves

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `EmailValidator#validate_each` calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` during user validation (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does a DB write as a side effect (`record.match_count += 1`, `record.last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) whenever a matching `blocked_emails` row exists, even if the user being validated never gets saved. This is a real, diff-grounded concern about validation having persistence side effects, though it may be intentional for tracking and not necessarily a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Two simultaneous signup attempts for the same blocked email both read and write back match_count, causing a lost update with no concurrency guard, making match statistics unreliable

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code does a read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save`) with no locking or atomic update. Under concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked email, two processes can read the same `match_count` and both write back `+1`, losing one increment, making `match_count`/`last_match_at` statistics unreliable.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Lookup case-sensitivity differs between old and new blocking mechanisms: legacy blacklist matched case-insensitively but BlockedEmail.where(email: email) in PostgreSQL is case-sensitive, so blocked rows can be bypassed via case variation

adjudication.rationale: The new blocking check in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does an exact equality lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) and the DB index is on `:email` without any case-insensitive handling. In PostgreSQL this is case-sensitive for a normal `string/varchar` column, so a blocked entry like `bad@spam.com` would not match `Bad@Spam.com` (or other case variants), allowing bypass. The diff does not show any normalization (e.g., downcasing) before this lookup, so the issue is exposed by the introduced mechanism.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No migration exists to normalize email case on load into blocked_emails, making the case-sensitivity drift undetectable until someone evades a block

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) does an exact-match query (`where(email: email).first`) and neither BlockedEmail nor EmailValidator normalizes case (e.g., downcases) before storing or comparing. The migration creates `blocked_emails.email` as a plain string with a unique index, and the model validates uniqueness without `case_sensitive: false`. On case-sensitive DBs (e.g., Postgres), `BlockedEmail` entries like `Bad@spam.com` will not block `bad@spam.com`, allowing simple case-variant evasion. The finding’s mention of a migration is a bit misfocused, but the underlying case-normalization gap is real and diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs DB read-then-write inside model validator with bare record.save whose failure is silently swallowed, undercounting block-rate telemetry

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (new `app/models/blocked_email.rb`), it does a read (`where(...).first`) then mutates stats and calls `record.save` without checking the return value or using `save!`. If `save` fails (validation/DB error), the failure is silently ignored and `match_count`/`last_match_at` won’t be persisted, while the method still returns the block decision based on `record.action_type`. This is a real, diff-grounded side-effect/telemetry correctness concern, not necessarily a functional blocking defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? mutates and persists BlockedEmail rows during validation of an unrelated record, inflating match_count/last_match_at on validation paths that never commit
matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe that the `should_block`/`should_block_email?` check is not a pure read: it mutates/persists `BlockedEmail` records by updating match statistics (`match_count`/`last_match_at`) during a blocking check, which is a misleading side effect and can be problematic under concurrency/validation paths.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blocked email lookup is an exact case-sensitive string match with no email normalization, allowing blocked users to register with case-variant addresses

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)`, the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is an exact match on the stored string. The diff shows no normalization/downcasing of `email` on input or storage for `BlockedEmail`, so case-variant addresses (e.g., `Bad@spam.com` vs `bad@spam.com`) would not match a blocked record in a case-sensitive DB comparison (typical for Postgres), allowing bypass of the new blocking logic in `EmailValidator`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client-side rejectedEmails.contains(email) is an exact string match with no trim/normalization, so the inline rejection hint only fires for byte-identical retries

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the new client-side shortcut checks `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` where `email` comes directly from `this.get("accountEmail")` and the stored value is `result.values.email` pushed via `pushObject`. The diff shows no trimming/case-normalization on either side, so the `contains` check is indeed an exact-string match and will only trigger the inline validation failure when the user re-enters the email byte-identically (e.g., not with different casing or incidental whitespace). Server-side validation still runs, so this is primarily a UX/edge-case concern rather than a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New errors/values payload shape depends on result.values being present; on failure paths like ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid the JS silently skips the rejection-memory push, making the feature partial

adjudication.rationale: The client-side “rejection memory” only triggers when the failure JSON includes both `errors.email` and `values` (`if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email) }`). The diff adds `errors`/`values` only in the normal validation-failure `else` branch of `UsersController#create`; other failure paths (e.g., the existing `rescue ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` path, whose response shape is not shown/updated here) may not include these keys, so the new feature will be incomplete for those cases (it will skip caching rejected emails).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Regexp.new builds a regex from raw admin-entered email_domains_blacklist text with no RegexpError guard, turning malformed config into site-wide 500s on all signups

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, email_in_restriction_setting? builds a Regexp via `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` from raw `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist` after only `gsub('.', '\\.')`. If an admin enters other regex metacharacters (e.g. `[` or unbalanced parens), `Regexp.new` can raise RegexpError during validation, causing signup/user creation to 500. There is no guard/rescue around Regexp.new.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New spec file tests neither the regex construction nor the blacklist/whitelist branches, leaving a coverage gap on the only non-trivial logic added

adjudication.rationale: The new validator logic in lib/validators/email_validator.rb adds non-trivial branches for SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist and regex-based matching via email_in_restriction_setting?. The new spec spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and asserts presence/absence of errors for the blocked-email path, without exercising the whitelist/blacklist branches or validating the regex matching behavior, leaving those added paths untested.
